summary: A 1970 note on padding by Steve Crocker. It is updated by RFC 228. Padding means extra filler bits added to messages.

eli5.summary: Sometimes messages need filler so they fit a required size, like adding extra paper to fill a box.

subtitle: How to find the end-of-message padding bit in a machine word with a few logical operations and a lookup table.

tldr.problem: Message padding is a 1 followed by zeros, and hosts must find the position of that 1 bit in a word, which is an unpleasant coding task if done bit by bit.
tldr.mechanism: Isolate the low-order 1 bit with W AND -W, then find its position by dividing the single-bit value by a well-chosen number p and looking up the remainder in a table.
tldr.outcome: A useful divisor p is a little larger than the word length, and the note supplies tables of good divisors and a Fortran program that finds them. It was updated by RFC 228.

sections.title: The Padding Problem
sections.content:
In this note Steve Crocker explains that the padding on a message is a string of the form 10*, that is, a 1 followed by zero or more 0 bits. For hosts with word lengths of 16, 32, 48 and so on, the padding is necessarily in the last word received from the IMP. For hosts with other word lengths of at least 16 bits, the 1 bit is in either the last word or the next to last word, and in the second case the last word is all zero.

The unpleasant part is finding the bit position of that 1 within its word. The obvious approach is to test the low-order bit repeatedly and shift right while it is zero. The note offers more pleasant techniques.
sections.eli5: Messages end with a 1 and then blank space. The hard part is finding where that last 1 sits.

sections.title: Isolating the Bit and Finding Its Position
sections.content:
Assuming two's complement arithmetic, a nonzero word W ends in a 1 followed by k zeros. Then W AND W-1 removes the low-order 1 bit, and W AND -W isolates it, leaving a word with a single bit set.

To get that bit's position, the obvious options are shifting with tests or floating normalization hardware, such as the JFFO instruction on the PDP-10. Hexadecimal normalization, as on IBM 360 and XDS Sigma 7 machines, may not be convenient. The note instead divides: a word with a single bit on has the value 2^k, so if the divisor p makes 2^k mod p distinct for every k below the word length n, a table of length p maps each remainder to a bit position.
sections.eli5: First you cover up everything except the last switch. Then a quick arithmetic trick tells you which switch it was, using a small cheat sheet.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content: For a word length of n = 8 and a divisor of p = 11, the values of 2^k mod 11 for k from 0 to 7 are 1, 2, 4, 8, 5, 10, 9 and 7. These give a lookup table of length 11 from remainder to bit position, in which remainders 0, 3 and 6 never occur.
sections.eli5: For eight switches, dividing by 11 gives a different leftover for each switch. The leftover points to the switch number in the cheat sheet.

sections.title: Choosing a Good Divisor
sections.content:
The divisor should be as small as possible to keep the table short. It must produce at least n distinct remainders, and zero cannot be a useful remainder, so p must be at least one more than the word length. This bound is reached for some word lengths. Writing R(p) for the number of distinct remainders p produces, the note tabulates it for odd p up to 21, and shows that 7, 15, 17 and 21 are useless because smaller divisors generate more distinct remainders.

The list of useful divisors below 100 is 1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13, 19, 25, 29, 37, 53, 59, 61, 67 and 83. The note also proves facts about R(p), says even divisors are generally not useful, gives a Fortran program, run on the SEX system at UCLA, that generated the table, and ends with number theory about the order of 2 modulo p and Euler's totient.
sections.eli5: You want the smallest dividing number that still gives every switch its own leftover, so the cheat sheet stays short.
